readingInstruction: Read Psalm 130. It is a Song of Ascents and one of the penitential psalms. Notice how the psalm moves from the depths to hope, and what the psalmist waits for.
settingTheScene: Psalm 130 was sung by pilgrims as they climbed to Jerusalem. Martin Luther loved it and called it one of the “Pauline psalms” because it teaches justification by grace as clearly as Paul does. It is only eight verses. John Wesley is said to have heard it sung at St. Paul’s Cathedral on the afternoon of the day his heart was “strangely warmed” in 1738.
observation: “Out of the depths I cry to you, O LORD!” (v. 1).
“O Lord, hear my voice! Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my pleas for mercy!” (v. 2).
“If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?” (v. 3).
“But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared” (v. 4).
“I wait for the LORD, my soul waits, and in his word I hope” (v. 5).
“My soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen for the morning” (v. 6).
“For with the LORD there is steadfast love, and with him is plentiful redemption” (v. 7).
“And he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities” (v. 8).
interpretation:
The psalm begins at the bottom: “Out of the depths I cry to you, O LORD!” The depths are deep waters, a place of overwhelming trouble. The psalm makes clear that the deepest trouble is sin. The psalmist cries for mercy, aware that he has no claim on God.

The question in verse 3 is among the most searching in the Bible: “If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?” The answer is no one. If God kept a record of every sin, no one would survive. This is Romans 3: none is righteous, no, not one. But the psalm turns on one word, “But.” “But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared.” The forgiveness is not a contradiction of God’s holiness. It is the result of his character. And the effect of forgiveness is not carelessness but reverence. The more we understand the cost of forgiveness, the more we fear God in the right way, with awe and love.

Next the psalmist waits. “I wait for the LORD, my soul waits, and in his word I hope.” He has no other support. He waits “more than watchmen for the morning,” repeated for emphasis. A night watchman on a city wall knows that morning will come, and longs for it. So the believer waits with certain hope for the LORD. Notice that hope is rooted in his word. The promises of God are the ground of waiting.

Then the psalmist turns to the whole community. “O Israel, hope in the LORD! For with the LORD there is steadfast love, and with him is plentiful redemption.” The word “plentiful” means abundant, overflowing. There is more redemption in God than sin in us. “And he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.” All of them. For us, this promise has been fulfilled at the cross. Jesus’ name means “he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). The plentiful redemption has been paid.

The psalm moves from the depths to the dawn. Many Christians have prayed it in seasons of guilt, depression, and delay. It teaches us that the way out of the depths is to cry to the LORD, to cling to his forgiveness, and to wait for him with hope.
connection: Psalm 51 and Psalm 32 are other penitential psalms. Exodus 34:6-7 tells of the LORD who forgives iniquity. Micah 7:18-19 asks who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity. Isaiah 40:31 speaks of those who wait on the LORD. Lamentations 3:25-26 says the LORD is good to those who wait for him. Matthew 1:21 gives the meaning of Jesus’ name. Titus 2:14 says Christ gave himself to redeem us from all lawlessness. Ephesians 1:7 says we have redemption through his blood. 1 Peter 1:18-19 speaks of the precious blood of Christ.
application:
Pray this psalm if you are in a low place. If you are not, pray it for someone who is.

Wait on the LORD in one area today without rushing. Let his word be your hope.

Count the gifts of redemption you have received in Christ.
prayerPrompts: Cry to God out of the depths.
Thank him that with him there is forgiveness and plentiful redemption.
Wait for him and trust his word.
